pages.name: A mix of two arrows
pages.text: Here are two arrows, `u = (2, 1)` and `v = (1, 3)`. A mix lays so many of each nose to tail. Two lots of u and one of v land on `(5, 5)`. The faint slanted grid has a line for every whole amount of u and of v. So whole amounts land on its corners.

pages.name: Land on a point
pages.task: Which amounts of u and v land on `(−1, 2)`?
pages.why: A negative amount turns an arrow round. So −1 lot of u is `(−2, −1)`. One v on the end adds `(1, 3)`. That lands on `(−1, 2)`.

pages.name: The span
pages.text: Every point a mix can reach is the arrows' [[span]]. The paint shades it, for amounts from −5 to 5. Each cell of the slanted grid is a parallelogram with u and v as its sides. Its area is the determinant, `2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5`. Amounts in between reach the points inside each cell. Cells with real area tile the plane with no gaps. So the span is the whole plane, and the paint covers the whole view.

pages.name: Line them up
pages.text: Now v swings round onto u's line, to `(−4, −2)`. That arrow is −2 lots of u. So any mix of the two is just some amount of u. The cells thin to nothing. Their area is `2 × (−2) − 1 × (−4) = 0`. The reach collapses to a line, because v adds no new direction. And `2u + 1v` lands on `(0, 0)`.

pages.name: Independent or not
pages.text: Here are the two pairs side by side. u and v make cells of area 5. Cells with real area give each point just one mix. So zero can only be `0u + 0v`. They are [[linearly independent]]. u and `(−4, −2)` make cells of area 0. `2u + (−4, −2)` lands on zero. Move `(−4, −2)` across, and it is `−2u`, on u's line. They are dependent, the opposite of independent.

pages.name: A third arrow
pages.text: In space, `u = (1, 0, −1)` and `v = (0, 2, −1)` span a flat sheet through the origin. A third arrow, w, makes a box with them. At first w sits off the sheet, and the box has volume 2. As w sinks to `(1, 2, −2) = u + v`, the box flattens. The span stays that sheet. To test by hand, put the arrows in as columns and solve `a u + b v + c w = 0`. All zeros always works, so it is never inconsistent. A free letter means dependent.

pages.name: Read the staircase
pages.task: Elimination of `a u + b v + c w = 0` for u, v and `w = (1, 2, −2)` ends in this staircase. What does it say about the arrows?
pages.answer: Dependent, as c is free, so a mix that is not all zeros gives zero
pages.why: Row 2 says `2b + 2c = 0`, and row 1 says `a + c = 0`. So c is free. Set `c = −1`. Then `a = 1` and `b = 1`. So `u + v − w` lands on zero, and the three are dependent.

pages.name: A basis
pages.text: A [[basis]] is a set of independent arrows that spans a space. i and j are one basis for the plane. `u = (2, 1)` and `v = (1, 3)` are another. Each pair makes cells with real area, so it spans the plane. A third arrow in the plane is always a mix of them. Three-phase phasors L1 and L2 span the plane, and `L1 + L2 + L3 = 0`. Next, you will swap one basis for another.

pages.why: Row 3 says `c = 0`. Then row 2 gives `b = 0`, and row 1 gives `a = 0`. Only all zeros works. The box they make has volume 1, not 0.

pages.name: Mixed: a basis
pages.task: Which set is a basis for the plane?
pages.why: `(3, 1)` and `(1, 1)` have determinant `3 × 1 − 1 × 1 = 2`. That is not 0, so they are independent. Their cells tile the plane, so they span it. Independent and spanning makes a basis.
